Why do you won't Trump release his tax returns?

They're going to look outrageously low because of the nature of his primary business; real estate investment. And if he has to explain why that is it's going to raise class inequality issues that affect his 'base'. You see, real estate investors don't usually make money on the use of their buildings. They operate their buildings to break-even on the cost of their maintenance. They make money on the periodic refinancing of their buildings as property values grow from the influence their buildings have on the market. So they take their profit from the proceeds of loans, which isn't taxable. Trump's holdings are likely a lot more complicated than that, but that's the basic principle of real estate investment. If you're a big shot in that line of work, you simply don't pay the level of personal taxes normal people pay because your income is coming out of credit. You're borrowing on the future value of your holdings. Real estate is, fundamentally, a Ponzi scheme, and always has been, and the people at the top of the racket usually don't want the public looking too closely at how it works.

Additionally, Trump cultivates his celebrity, his 'brand', as a tool to influence the market. Real estate values do not rise by simple market rules. It's not all about people actually needing to live or setup shop in a particular place for economically rational reasons. There are other influences like the 'character' of a place, the aesthetic of the surrounding architecture, the prestige associated with it. Sometimes it's just idiots following the herd. Frankly, investors aren't particularly rational or intelligent people. Their decision-making processes often come down to a lot of subjective and magical thinking--a lot of voodoo economics--and they often get caught by the Greater Fool Syndrome and Sunk Cost Fallacy.

A Trump building, because of the celebrity he's engineered, has more prestige than a normal building and that translates to more capital to build it with, a bigger increase in property value growth both on the building and around it, and more people wanting an address there. And so he can refinance sooner and/or for more money. Trump's success relies on people foolishly thinking that he has some magical business acumen, some special insight, and so he capitalizes on their confidence. He's successful not for anything he's actually done but for what people believe he can do. Real estate is all about capital, and capital is all about the confidence associated with class and celebrity. Trump often just exploits his brand alone, lending it to buildings and projects he doesn't actually own but getting a cut on the value his name has added to a project. Most real estate investors don't want a high profile. Just a few manage to do personal brand cultivation well, sometimes specializing in certain areas of development and making themselves out to be some kind of real estate development 'artist'. One example is Steve Wynn, famous for his hotels, resorts, and casinos.

I suspect Trump plans to do for/to America exactly what he does in real estate.

Certain conditions usually combine to thrust We The People into a state of social unrest and desperation. What is born from that suffering is what we must learn from and understand as a safeguard to keep ourselves from such future circumstances. Our Constitution provides us a way to achieve what Iceland had to do in free form. Their methods successful, however unplanned the steps to get there may have been. If The Powers That Be have their formula for control, We The People have one for reclamation. However imperfect, Iceland has led the way and the following is their history of struggle and victory over those who sought to oppress and exploit.

Iceland is a small country with a population around 320,000 people. In 2008, when the world was feeling the damages caused from fiscal irresponsibility, they saw a need and rushed to fill it. Their government had become robust. So much so that it began putting The Powers That Be well being ahead of it's own peoples' needs. Upending the social construct of an elected few ruling unjustly over the vast majority.

Since finance lit this fire, finance is where we will begin. Federal governments grow to useless and bureaucratic entities when left to their own designs. For within chaos resides opportunity. And opportunity can be exploited for more power.

Corporate tax rates were at an abysmal 18% while the people adhered to a fixed tax rate of 36%, regardless of income. So, if you lived in Iceland in 2008, earned $100 a year, you'd be paying $36 (over one-third of all income) towards an ever growing government. This alone should display how divided and unequal the social factions had become in Iceland.

We must first understand how Iceland arrived at this point of exploitation. To understand the force behind their desperation, let's start with what ultimately caused the financial fiasco: Deregulation. This is where an industry, having the need for certain rules, laws, regulations and/or guidelines benefit from the removal of civilian and/or governmental oversight. This ability for an industry to say they no longer need regulations came from the economic philosophy which saw inefficiencies of government bureaucracy in the form of regulations becoming counterproductive. More so than that was the idea that the industry could become self-regulating by controlling the very regulatory agencies designed to limit that very industry.

In fear of an industry being able to move unchecked through bureaucratic control, they DEREGULATED the banking industry in 2001. Now, outside of a healthy purview, the banks could be as irresponsible as they deemed necessary. Bankers love money. Greed gives way to more greed so whichever way the bankers could make more money, they would make it. Regardless of financial risk.

In this specific situation, the problem arose from 3 Icelandic banks: Kaupthing, Landsbanki and Glitnir. Due to the deregulation, the years leading up to the KR, the banks multiplied in size. They were able to do so by the readily accessible credit found in the international financial market. Specifically the short-term financing. When the international financial crisis hit in 2007/2008, investors saw Iceland's banks increasingly risky - untrustworthy. When trust in the banks fell, the value of their currency - the krona - sharply fell. In 2008 in became significantly more difficult for the banks to roll over the short-term debt they so easily gave away in years prior. The end of the second quarter of the fiscal year 2008 saw Iceland's external debt (debt to foreign creditors) at 9.5 trillion kronur. Which was over seven times the GDP (Gross Domestic Profit). They had more debt than money being made yearly. The 3 banks had a total assets value of 14.4 trillion kronur, which at the end of the second quarter 2008, was eleven times the national GDP. So with the Icelandic financial system dwarfing the actively producing economy, The Central Bank of Iceland was incapable of leading more debt due to the mismatched sizes of their financial system. If a bank has it's hands tied and unable to pay debts owed, there can be no trust in those banks. On the sixth of October, the Icelandic legislature instituted an emergency law enabling the Financial Supervisory Authority to take control over financial institutions and from the banks own priority claims, the FSA made domestic deposits in an attempt toe keep them solvent.

Afterwards, new banks were made to take over the domestic operations of Kaupthing, Landsbanki and Glitnir. The 3 banks defaulted, unable to pay owed debts, and as a result, shareholders and foreign creditors lost their investments. Attempts to stabilize the financial crisis were made. The IMF (International Monetary Fund) and a coalition of Nordic countries created a US$5.1 billion sovereign debt package to ultimately restore their national banking systems.

The damage was done, though. Currency values plummeted. Foreign currency transactions virtually suspended and the Icelandic stock exchange fell by more than 90%.

So girlfriend and I are starting to think Poland seems like the only place in Europe that is getting it right with regards to immigrants. And we are considering moving there before "shit hits the fan" in Germany, and hordes of Germans are fleeing towards the Polish-German border as the civil war in Germany worsens. Because one thing is for sure, if something like that happens in Germany, Poland isn't going to let anyone in.

If you live in Poland or are moving there, what are some things the expat should know about, cultural differences we should make ourselves acquainted with, other advises?
Anyone moving to Poland, or living there?

I'm from Czechia, the southern neighbour of Poland who along with the rest of the V4 countries (Slovakia and Hungary) are fairly united in the rejection of refugees and Islam. I think Poland is an up and coming county but Czechia is better in many aspects and you could consider moving here. We are still a very homogeneous country, there are some bigger immigrant communities but it's mostly other Slavs or the Vietnamese who are pretty chill. Czechs are fairly united against Islam and there is a dislike of third world migration, Prague has the right kind of cosmopolitanism (i.e. you can get foreign food and stuff but there are no ghettos or immigrant areas, other than some places with a lot of Russians. I estimate Prague is probably around 95% white whereas the rest of the country is probably a solid 98%, just my estimates though). People in Prague are fairly accepting of expats, and since you are a foreigner that is something you should look for. Poland is more hostile to foreigners. Here is a short list of pros/cons.

Pros:

  • Very low unemployment

  • Cheap

  • Lots of things to do

  • Great public transportation system (Prague)

  • Best beer in the world (sorry Germans) that is incredibly cheap

  • Weed is easy to find and if the cops catch you all you get is a fine (unless you have more than 10g iirc)

  • Tons of historical buildings everywhere

  • Safe

  • Very homogeneous

  • Very secular, most people are irreligious or atheists

Cons:

  • Wages can be low, but it depends where you work

  • Inefficient bureaucracy (but then again that is true for most countries)

  • The typical czech cuisine in my opinion isn't very good, luckily there are tons of restaurants with food from all over the world

  • Corruption

The plus sides:

  • Property is dirt cheap. Not sure of the legalities for non-citizens, but everybody there buys and nobody rents. Buying a plot, and building to your own specifications costs just as much, and often less, than buying something already built. Don't plan on renting it out later as you won't find renters, unless you're in a university town.

  • Cars are dirt cheap

  • Fuel is affordable
  • Food is amazing, particularly as most of it is still sold in old market-style farmers markets, usually veg plucked from the ground or chicken that was slaughtered that very morning, and mostly organic :-) Many small, local shops carry small varieties of fresh foods as well. When you buy bread in the morning, it's still warm from the oven most of the time. Supermarkets are of course also available, but such a waste when such amazing foods are available elsewhere.
  • The people and the culture are the most non-PC ever, and it's awesome.
  • Millenials are pretty non-religious but were raised catholic, their parents were raised more strongly catholic, and their grandparents are very catholic.

Minuses:

  • The economy is shit. You will see a lot of poverty. Many families still live in 2-3 generation homes, with grandparents, parents, or kids generations all together. However, they do tend to be tidy, quiet, and polite, even if really poor, and families always help eachother.
  • There is an alcoholism problem. There are a lot of heavy alcoholics. Every family has a drunkard uncle.
  • There is a major, major lack of employment. Sometimes, just one or two members of multi generation households can find work. Although most manage to pay off or inherit the homes they live in, they are usually supporting a lot of people. Unemployment benefits are completely minimal and no one could ever survive on them, if they are even lucky enough to get them which is quite difficult
  • Welfare is very minimal. Even the severely disabled have trouble getting welfare, and if they do receive it, the amount is tiny. There is a large amount of poverty because this is coupled with a total job shortage.
  • Worker's rights are non-existent. Even major companies will under-pay, or pay their workers late, and many heavy labour factory jobs have inhumane hours, like 60-80 hour workweeks are common. This is usually done partially off-the-books, because the government is unfriendly to businesses as it is, and they can't afford to pay both overtime and the excessive taxes.
  • Poland is unfriendly to business as well. VAT is high, Zus (social security) is high and paid at a flat rate no matter what the income. This means workers with few hours can cost their bosses more than their paycheck in taxes. Bosses are taxed to death in many other ways and administrative fees as well, and can't afford to pay something like overtime
  • Poor people have insane work ethics and are often grateful for 60-80 hour workweeks, most are just happy to have a job at all. This is total bullshit, but it would really help if the government stopped taxing every business and every employee to death. There is a lot of black market work completely off the books simply because of the high charges for both businesses and workers. This, of course, leads to inhumane working conditions in some of the factories.

The general culture

  • There is a lot of 'doing things through friends', so network like hell. Anything you need taken care of will go much easier if you have a friend in the industry, whether it's paperwork, banking, or business, literally anything will be easier if you have friends involved. By the way, when you visit them at home and they are doing you a favor, bring chocolates or even champagne in the case of bigger business ventures.
  • They love other Europeans and Americans. They're neutral towards jews. They hate gypsies and muslims. They will not even try to be polite or politically correct about this.
  • A lot of stuff is still done under the table and off the books in general. There is still a lot of corruption in a lot of places, money and gifts can sometimes (but not always) help facilitate getting something done. Some (not all) Doctors, for example, often will treat patients better when paid tips, and sometimes worse if no tip is offered. You used to be able to buy drivers licensees, it's less common now, but some employees still do it. That also goes for other types of paperwork.
  • National healthcare is shit, private is much better. Avoid hospitals at all costs, even healthy people die there sometimes.

Haha, I sound a little doom and gloom but it's actually much better than I'm making it sound. I'd say it's become more western nowadays, more families can afford to live on their own, the houses are well maintained and often newly built in very modern styles, many people do have steady jobs with pensions, and most are not corrupt. I just wanted to note that the dark side is still there a little bit, you know, leftover from the socialist times, and there are still no financial safety nets.

There's a lot of drinking and being merry, a lot of closely knit families, a lot of home cooked meals, and a lot of loyal friends. Many young people are feeding money into the economy working from other countries, and I have faith they will be returning home at some point to boost that economy further. I have hopes the government will decide to cash in on being more business-friendly, as that would change everything as people return. If you have a foreign income, you will do very very well, as cost of living is dirt cheap and so is property. You'll find many new friends, good beer, and the most delicious food.

A few days ago, I visited my 65-year old father and we sat on his balcony for hours, drinking wine and talking about everything. It's something special for me, our relationship really started to blossom only a few years ago and I'm happy to see that we both didn't stop learning things.

When he was young, my father was absolutely fit. He had a black belt in Karate and Judo, played soccer and trained soccer teams. Some time ago, he had his first bout of gout and got diagnosed with thrombocytosis. It's basically cancer, but "luckily" a form which doesn't metastasize and can be controlled with medication quite well, considering. Even more reasons to be glad about our improving relationship.

Back to to the balcony; we sat there and I told him about my obese coworker and how his fat rules over every bit of his life and the lives of persons in contact with him. All of a sudden, my father switched to ultimate shitlord mode and let all his disgust for fat people out at once. He's completely oblivious to the depths of the internet, but he sounded like he ate FPH for breakfast. How disgustingly lazy fat people were, how atrocious they smelled, how warped their perception was, how they laid on the shoulders of society, how they ruined a feat of evolution with their uncontrolled impulsivity, how they failed to walk 100 meters and still call themselves perfect, how disgustig panniculi and fat asses and rolls looked and how much of a health problem they are, how LESS of a human a fat person was because he failed at doing basic human things, how they still wobbled to McDonald's and didn't think they had a problem when they couldn't see their feet anymore.

He went on with several examples from his working life. He was working with children from problematic families and had seen it all, 7-year old alcoholics and smokers, and of course, morbidly obese children. Parents thought it was okay to pack their first-graders THREE breakfasts because "they were so hungry". Everything he said came full circle now, and I thought about how often FPH comes to the same conclusion.
